accepted.s: According to Census 2011, the urban population of India was approximately
accepted.x: Census 2011 recorded India’s urban population at approximately 37.71 crore, or 377.1 million.
accepted.tq: Use the exact population figure rather than confusing it with the urbanisation percentage.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly represents India’s rural and urban population shares according to Census 2011?
accepted.x: In Census 2011, 68.84% of India’s population was rural and 31.16% was urban.
accepted.tq: Split the paired rural–urban percentages carefully.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s: India’s level of urbanisation increased from 27.81% in 2001 to approximately what level in 2011?
accepted.x: The urbanisation rate rose from 27.81% in 2001 to 31.16% in 2011.
accepted.tq: Compare the two census percentages and identify the later figure.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the spatial importance of Indian cities:
1. Cities occupy about 3% of India’s land area.
2. Cities account for about 60% of India’s GDP.
3. Urban population is projected to reach approximately 60 crore by 2031.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct: cities occupy about 3% of land, generate around 60% of GDP, and the urban population is projected to reach about 60 crore by 2031.
accepted.tq: Test a compact group of related quantitative statements.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The 16th Finance Commission projects India’s urbanisation level to reach approximately what percentage by 2031?
accepted.x: The 16th Finance Commission projects urbanisation at approximately 41% by 2031.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the projected percentage from the Census 2011 level.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the least urbanised southern State referred to in the comparative data?
accepted.x: Andhra Pradesh, in the undivided-State comparison, had the lowest urbanisation level at about 33%, compared with Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
accepted.tq: Use the comparison figures to separate the similar southern-State options.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which State recorded the highest decadal growth of urban population during 2001–2011?
accepted.x: Sikkim recorded the highest decadal growth of urban population during 2001–2011.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between a growth-rate fact and an urbanisation-level fact.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Arrange the following phases of urbanisation in India in chronological order:
A. Rapid phase
B. Medium phase
C. Slow phase

Select the correct answer.
accepted.x: The slow phase occurred during 1901–1931, the medium phase during 1931–1961, and the rapid phase from 1961 onwards.
accepted.tq: Identify the time ranges and arrange the phases from earliest to latest.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s: During which period did India experience the slow phase of urbanisation, when the urban share remained around 10.8% to 12%?
accepted.x: The slow phase of Indian urbanisation occurred between 1901 and 1931, when the urban share rose only from about 10.8% to 12%.
accepted.tq: Match the phase with its specific period and numerical range.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly describes the medium phase of urbanisation in India?
o: The urban share increased from 27.81% to 31.16% during 1961–1991.
The urban share increased from about 12% to 18% during 1931–1961.
The urban share remained constant at about 10% during 1931–1961.
accepted.x: The medium phase extended from 1931 to 1961, during which the urban share increased from about 12% to 18%.
accepted.tq: Reject reversed trends and match the correct period with its figures.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The term ‘hidden urbanisation’ in the Indian context is associated with the estimate that India is approximately what percentage urban according to DEGURBA-based estimates?
accepted.x: DEGURBA-based estimates cited by the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister put India at about 63% urban, much higher than the Census figure.
accepted.tq: Distinguish an alternative spatial estimate from the official Census percentage.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s: According to the Economic Survey 2025–26, what is the approximate effect of doubling city size on productivity?
accepted.x: The Economic Survey 2025–26 states that doubling city size lifts productivity by approximately 12%.
accepted.tq: Test the precise quantitative relationship rather than a broad urbanisation trend.
accepted.sec: Urbanisation trends - Census 2011 share, most/least urbanised States, fastest growth, AP  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements regarding global urbanisation is correct?
o: India alone accounts for more than half of the world’s urban population.
Less than one-fourth of the world’s population is already urban.
The world will become completely urban by 2030.
More than half of the world’s population is already urban.
accepted.x: More than half of the world’s population is already living in urban areas.
accepted.tq: Identify the carefully worded global trend statement.
accepted.sec: Global urbanisation projections - UN World Urbanization Prospects  [APPSC]

accepted.s: India’s cities are expected to accommodate nearly how many people by 2050 according to the cited projection?
accepted.x: India’s cities are projected to host nearly one billion people by 2050; the cited approximation is about 900 million.
accepted.tq: Convert the approximate phrase ‘nearly a billion’ into the closest option.
accepted.sec: Global urbanisation projections - UN World Urbanization Prospects  [APPSC]

accepted.s: A settlement is treated as a statutory town when it is
o: any settlement classified as urban by an international agency
notified under State law and provided with an urban local body
an area where 75% of male workers are engaged in non-agricultural activities
a village with a population exceeding 5,000 and density above 400 persons per square kilometre
accepted.x: A statutory town is notified under State law and has an urban local body such as a corporation, municipality, nagar panchayat or cantonment board.
accepted.tq: Separate statutory status from the three demographic criteria of a Census town.
accepted.sec: Urban settlement classification - census vs statutory towns, size classes, million-plus  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT a criterion for identifying a Census town in India?
o: At least 75% of male main workers engaged in non-agricultural activities
Presence of a municipal corporation constituted under State law
Population density of at least 400 persons per square kilometre
accepted.x: A municipal corporation is characteristic of a statutory town. A Census town is identified administratively as a village using the population, occupational and density criteria.
accepted.tq: Find the statutory-town feature among the Census-town criteria.
accepted.sec: Urban settlement classification - census vs statutory towns, size classes, million-plus  [other exams]

accepted.s: The criteria for Census towns have remained unchanged since
accepted.x: The criteria for Census towns have remained unchanged since 1981.
accepted.tq: Test the specific base year associated with the classification criteria.
accepted.sec: Urban settlement classification - census vs statutory towns, size classes, million-plus  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Census towns:
1. They are administratively villages.
2. They must have a population of at least 5,000.
3. They must have a density of at least 400 persons per square kilometre.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: A Census town remains administratively a village but satisfies all three specified demographic and occupational conditions, including the separate requirement that 75% of male workers be non-agricultural.
accepted.tq: Combine the definition with its threshold criteria.
accepted.sec: Urban settlement classification - census vs statutory towns, size classes, million-plus  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the approximate composition of India’s towns in 2011?
accepted.x: India had approximately 4,041 statutory towns and 3,892 Census towns in 2011, giving a total of about 7,933 towns.
accepted.tq: Keep the two categories in their correct order and compare their approximate counts.
accepted.sec: Urban settlement classification - census vs statutory towns, size classes, million-plus  [other exams]

accepted.s: How many population-size classes are used in the Census classification of Indian towns?
accepted.x: Indian towns are classified into six population-size classes, from Class I to Class VI.
accepted.tq: Recall the number of categories rather than the thresholds of one category.
accepted.sec: Urban settlement classification - census vs statutory towns, size classes, million-plus  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly matches a Census town class with its population range?
accepted.x: Class I towns have 1 lakh or more population, Class II towns have 50,000–99,999, Class III 20,000–49,999, Class IV 10,000–19,999, Class V 5,000–9,999 and Class VI below 5,000.
accepted.tq: Start with the sure population interval and eliminate shifted class labels.
accepted.sec: Urban settlement classification - census vs statutory towns, size classes, million-plus  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which State has the largest number of towns in India?
accepted.x: Tamil Nadu has the largest number of towns among Indian States.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the State with the most towns from the State with the largest urban population.
accepted.sec: Urban settlement classification - census vs statutory towns, size classes, million-plus  [other exams]

accepted.s: India ranks third in the world in terms of absolute urban population, after
accepted.x: India has the world’s third-largest absolute urban population, after China and the United States.
accepted.tq: Use the ranking order rather than the level of urbanisation.
accepted.sec: Urban settlement classification - census vs statutory towns, size classes, million-plus  [other exams]

accepted.s: The largest urban agglomerations among the following are correctly arranged in descending order as
accepted.x: The largest urban agglomerations listed are Greater Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata in that order.
accepted.tq: Apply descending-order comparison to the three named urban agglomerations.
accepted.sec: Urban settlement classification - census vs statutory towns, size classes, million-plus  [other exams]

accepted.s: The World Bank estimate cited for the number of slum dwellers in India is approximately
accepted.x: The cited World Bank estimate places India’s slum-dwelling population at approximately 177 million, the largest such population in the world.
accepted.tq: Separate the exact estimate from nearby rounded alternatives.
accepted.sec: Urban challenges - housing, slums, transport, waste, water  [other exams]

accepted.s: According to Census 2011 data cited for million-plus cities, which city had the highest proportion of its population living in slums?
accepted.x: Greater Visakhapatnam had the highest cited slum share among million-plus cities, at approximately 44%, compared with about 41% in Greater Mumbai and Vijayawada.
accepted.tq: Compare close percentages instead of selecting the more famous city.
accepted.sec: Urban challenges - housing, slums, transport, waste, water  [other exams]

accepted.s: The estimated urban housing shortage identified by the Technical Group in 2012 was approximately
accepted.x: The Technical Group estimated India’s urban housing shortage at approximately 18.78 million units in 2012.
accepted.tq: Read the decimal figure carefully and avoid shifting the leading digit.
accepted.sec: Urban challenges - housing, slums, transport, waste, water  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a major transport challenge in Indian cities?
o: Universal availability of high-capacity public transport
accepted.x: Private-vehicle preference, congestion and weak public transport are identified challenges. Universal availability of high-capacity public transport is not a stated challenge.
accepted.tq: Find the option that reverses the problem into a solution.
accepted.sec: Urban challenges - housing, slums, transport, waste, water  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which one of the following best explains why municipalities face difficulty in managing urban solid waste?
o: Municipalities are overwhelmed by the volume and management demands of solid waste.
Waste generation is confined to statutory towns only.
Solid waste is managed exclusively by rural panchayats.
Urban areas generate no biodegradable waste.
accepted.x: Municipalities are overwhelmed by the increasing volume and operational requirements of solid-waste management.
accepted.tq: Identify the option that states the practical governance challenge without an extreme claim.
accepted.sec: Urban challenges - housing, slums, transport, waste, water  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding emerging urban environmental risks:
1. About two-thirds of urban dwellers may face pluvial flooding by 2030.
2. The urban heat-island effect may raise temperatures by about 3–5°C.
3. These risks are unrelated to urban planning.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: About two-thirds of urban dwellers may face pluvial flooding by 2030, and the urban heat-island effect is estimated at about 3–5°C. The risks are closely connected with urban planning and infrastructure.
accepted.tq: Reject the absolute causal denial in statement 3 while retaining the two quantified risks.
accepted.sec: Urban challenges - housing, slums, transport, waste, water  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which one of the following is a governance-related urban challenge identified in India?
o: Complete fiscal autonomy of all cities
Absence of any panchayats in rapidly urbanising areas
Uniform administrative control over all urban local bodies
Fragmented authority and limited fiscal autonomy of cities
accepted.x: Fragmented authority and inadequate fiscal autonomy constrain city governance. Rapidly urbanising areas may also remain under panchayat administration.
accepted.tq: Use the governance lens to identify the institutional constraint.
accepted.sec: Urban challenges - housing, slums, transport, waste, water  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Which of the following correctly distinguishes push and pull factors of urbanisation?
1. Rural unemployment is a push factor.
2. Urban employment opportunities are a pull factor.
3. Better urban amenities may act as a pull factor.
4. Monsoon failure can push rural workers towards cities.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: Rural unemployment and monsoon failure push people out of rural areas, while urban employment and amenities attract them to cities.
accepted.tq: Classify each factor as either an outward push or an urban pull.
accepted.sec: Causes of urbanisation - push and pull  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the major component of urbanisation in India when natural increase in rural and urban areas is broadly similar?
accepted.x: Migration is the major component of urbanisation when natural increase in rural and urban areas is broadly similar.
accepted.tq: Identify the principal demographic component from the stated comparison.
accepted.sec: Causes of urbanisation - push and pull  [other exams]

accepted.s:
Which of the following factors can contribute to urbanisation through mechanisms other than migration?
1. Industrialisation
2. Commercialisation
3. Improved transport and communication
4. Reclassification of settlements as new towns
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: Industrialisation, commercialisation, transport and communication improvements, and reclassification as new towns can all increase urbanisation.
accepted.tq: Recognise the complete list when all listed structural factors support the process.
accepted.sec: Causes of urbanisation - push and pull  [other exams]

accepted.s: UN-Habitat, formally known as the UN Human Settlements Programme, was established in 1978 and has its headquarters at
accepted.x: UN-Habitat was established in 1978 and is headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya.
accepted.tq: Pair the organisation with its establishment year and headquarters.
accepted.sec: UN-Habitat and urban forums - Right to the City, APMCHUD  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which Sustainable Development Goal is most directly associated with UN-Habitat’s urban-settlement mandate?
accepted.x: SDG 11 seeks to make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable, directly corresponding to the UN-Habitat mandate.
accepted.tq: Match the specialised agency’s mandate with the relevant SDG.
accepted.sec: UN-Habitat and urban forums - Right to the City, APMCHUD  [other exams]

accepted.s: The concept of ‘Right to the City’ is associated with which thinker?
accepted.x: The concept of the Right to the City was articulated by Henri Lefebvre in 1968.
accepted.tq: Match the concept with its originator and associated year.
accepted.sec: UN-Habitat and urban forums - Right to the City, APMCHUD  [other exams]

accepted.s: The Right to the City was adopted in the New Urban Agenda at
accepted.x: The Right to the City was adopted in the New Urban Agenda at Habitat III, held in Quito in 2016.
accepted.tq: Match the forum, location and year without confusing the Habitat conferences.
accepted.sec: UN-Habitat and urban forums - Right to the City, APMCHUD  [other exams]

accepted.s: The first meeting of APMCHUD was held in
accepted.x: The first Asia-Pacific Ministerial Conference on Housing and Urban Development was held in New Delhi in 2006.
accepted.tq: Separate the inaugural forum’s location and year from other urban institutions and events.
accepted.sec: UN-Habitat and urban forums - Right to the City, APMCHUD  [other exams]

accepted.s: Under the AP–UN-Habitat Memorandum of Understanding of July 2026, the Centre of Excellence for Urban Affairs was proposed at
accepted.x: The AP–UN-Habitat MoU of July 2026 proposed a Centre of Excellence for Urban Affairs at Amaravati.
accepted.tq: Use the location-specific institutional fact and avoid substituting other major Andhra Pradesh cities.
accepted.sec: UN-Habitat and urban forums - Right to the City, APMCHUD  [other exams]

accepted.s: Which set of initiatives is supported by the AP–UN-Habitat MoU relating to the Centre of Excellence for Urban Affairs?
o: SURGE AP, RISE AP and UPLIFT AP
AMRUT AP, SMART AP and PMAY AP
RISE AP, SWACHH AP and JAL JEEVAN AP
SURGE AP, UDAY AP and GATI AP
accepted.x: The Centre of Excellence at Amaravati supports the initiatives named SURGE AP, RISE AP and UPLIFT AP.
accepted.tq: Start from the exact pair of programme names and eliminate substituted scheme titles.
